newsitem.title: PERU: Freed Japanese ambassador in Peru heads home.
newsitem.headline: Freed Japanese ambassador in Peru heads home.

text.p: Peru closed a symbolic chapter in its 18-week hostage siege on Sunday as Japan's Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, a former hostage and host of the ill-fated cocktail party overrun by leftist rebels, returned to Tokyo.

Waving goodbye to Peru from his wheelchair, Aoki boarded a Japan Airlines flight to Tokyo late on Saturday with his Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who had come to Lima to congratulate Peru's President Alberto Fujimori on the hostage rescue raid.
All but one of the 72 hostages trapped inside Aoki's grand residence in Lima were rescued alive by Peruvian army and navy commandos in a daring military strike last Tuesday.
The silver-haired Aoki, 58, is still confined to a wheelchair as he recovers from a hip injury sustained jumping out a second-story window while explosions and gunfire rocked the house.

Tokyo officials have not said if Aoki, said to be a charming and amusing host even after his party was crashed by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), will return to his post as envoy to Peru.

The veteran diplomat has apologised to his government and to Peru because the lavish reception he held in honour of Emperor Akihito's birthday turned into a four-month nightmare for the 72 men held hostage until Tuesday.
Aoki once joked it was the longest cocktail party he ever hosted.
He left Peru with his wife, as more details emerged about the cat-and-mouse game between the MRTA and Fujimori's government in the weeks before the raid.
Peruvian security forces managed to spy on the MRTA hostage-takers via listening devices scattered about the besieged home, with one device hidden inside a crucifix, military sources told Reuters.
Other bugs were hidden in a bible, a guitar, a chess piece and a crutch used by an MRTA guerrilla wounded in the initial takeover of the house, according to the Frecuencia Latina network.
Peruvian security forces said one hostage, retired navy Rear Adm. Luis Giampietri, once tested a listening device by speaking into it, "If you can hear me, tomorrow morning play a Mexican tune."
Sure enough, the next day police loudspeakers swapped their usual repertoire of military marches for a selection of Mexican folk songs, the sources said.

What was still unclear, news reports said, was how the government got the bugs into the house. Except for journalists early in the crisis, the only people allowed in were doctors, Red Cross workers and people involved in ultimately fruitless peace talks.

MRTA commander Nestor Cerpa grew over-confident in the last days of negotiations and was convinced that he was about to win release for some of the group's 450 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages, the newspaper La Republica said.

"Cerpa said that he had won the upper hand over the government," it quoted a source close to negotiations as saying. "He was saying that everything would turn out all right and that there would be no deaths."
Cerpa's bullet-ridden corpse was later seen sprawled on a staircase in television footage of the gutted and bombed-out house, next to those of two other dead guerrillas.

Cerpa's mother Felicitas Cartolini said she planned to sue the Japanese government for the death of her son because, under international law, the ambassador's residence is considered Japanese sovereign soil.

A poll issued on Sunday said 76 percent of Peruvians felt the raid had improved the country's image abroad, and 67 percent thought Fujimori's image had been strengthened. The survey by polling agency Analistas y Consultores was of 400 people and had a margin of error of 4.9 percent.
